intro:
Paul writes Philemon around AD 62 from prison in Rome—a personal letter about a runaway slave, Onesimus, who became a Christian under Paul's ministry. Onesimus ('useful') had apparently stolen from his master Philemon and fled to Rome, where he encountered Paul and converted. Now Paul sends him back with this tactful letter pleading for forgiveness and hinting at manumission.

Philemon is a wealthy Colossian Christian whose house hosts a church. Paul writes not as an apostle commanding but as 'an old man and now also a prisoner' appealing on the basis of love. The letter is a masterpiece of persuasion: Paul praises Philemon's character, offers to pay any debt, reminds him of his own spiritual debt to Paul, and suggests Onesimus' return is providential.

This shortest Pauline letter addresses slavery indirectly—not attacking the institution head-on but planting revolutionary seeds within Christian relationships. Paul treats Onesimus as a 'dear brother' rather than property, asking Philemon to receive him 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother.'
outro:
Paul ends with confidence in Philemon's obedience, requests preparation of a guest room (hinting at upcoming visit), and sends greetings from coworkers including Mark, Aristarchus, Luke, and Demas.

Philemon became a key text in the abolition movement, showing how the gospel undermines master-slave relationships by creating spiritual equality. Though Paul doesn't explicitly condemn slavery, he treats Onesimus with dignity and appeals to voluntary Christian brotherhood that makes slavery unthinkable among believers.

This personal letter demonstrates how the gospel transforms social relationships from within. Its combination of boldness and tact, principle and prudence, provides a model for addressing injustice through persuasion rather than coercion. The story of reconciliation between master and slave illustrates the 'ministry of reconciliation' Paul describes in 2 Corinthians.
